newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Rescuers x-ray debris for cavities, but no sign of.
newsitem.headline: Rescuers x-ray debris for cavities, but no sign of.

text.p: Rescuers on Tuesday x-rayed the concrete rubble of a six-day-old landslide at an Australian ski village, looking for cavities that might hide Eight people are still missing in the heap of broken concrete, twisted metal, dirt and timber, and last Saturday night's miraculous rescue of ski instructor Stuart Diver has kept alive hopes of finding more signs of life.

"There's always hope," police site commander Don Keene told reporters. "Overseas there's been people in situations like this for 10 days, so there's hope and we just keep driving on that hope that we will be successful."

Night temperatures at Thredbo village, 400 km (250 miles) south of Sydney, have plunged well below zero Celsius since two ski lodges were engulfed by the landslide on Wednesday night, trapping 19 people. So far, 10 bodies have been found.
The x-ray machines, which can penetrate the 30-cm thick (foot-thick) concrete, led rescuers on Tuesday to a cavity near the concrete tomb in which Diver, 27, lay trapped for 65 hours.
Rescue teams were burrowing by hand toward the cavity late on Tuesday night, extending the honeycomb of tunnels dug into the debris to a total about 25 metres (88 feet).
"There's a cavity above where Stuart Diver was," fire brigade superintendent Steve Hyman told reporters. "That's where we are heading with the tunnelling."
Police said they believed the eight missing people were trapped in one general area of the rubble.

Diver is recovering quickly in a hospital in Canberra, north of Thredbo, after minor surgery for frostbite to his feet. He was in bed with his wife, Sally, and wearing only boxer shorts when disaster struck.
It was near midnight when a steep hillside gave way, sending one ski lodge crashing into another below it.
The bodies of six men and four women have been recovered, the latest on Monday night.
But shifting rubble early on Tuesday cost rescuers precious hours in their race against the weather to find more survivors.
A big slab of concrete, one of several balancing precariously atop the debris, forced rescuers to scurry from the steep hillside for fear of another collapse.
"It could have toppled," police spokesman Mark Hargreaves told Reuters at Thredbo, in the picturesque Snowy Mountains.
Rescue efforts have been frustrated almost daily by the threat of further slippage. Approaching rain, forecast to arrive as early as Wednesday night, also weighed on rescuers' minds.
Rescuers on Tuesday night began erecting big tarpaulins over the disaster area to prevent rainfall from further destabilising the slope and flooding the tunnels they have painstakingly dug.
The small, tightly knit community of Thredbo on Tuesday began the slow and painful path to recovery, releasing a song to mark the disaster at this winter playground.
But villagers have begun to resent the harsh glare of the world's media, complaining that some journalists have been "pushy" and insensitive in reporting the extraordinary events.
Acting Prime Minister Tim Fischer wants the Press Council of Australia to investigate the complaints.
